description: A metal-working shop has access to two types of metal-working equipment, a chop saw and a steel cutter. A chop saw can work 25 pounds of steel and generates 25 units of waste every day. A steel cutter can only cut 5 pounds of steel and generates 3 units of waste every day.  The metal-working shop is expecting an increase in demand and must cut 520 pounds of metal every day. However, there is a waste limitation due to the fines that may be in place if too much heavy metal is discarded and they may at most produce 400 units of waste every day. How should the metal-working shop purchase their metal-working equipment to decrease the total number of metal-working equipment needed?

ChopSawCuttingCapacity.definition: Cutting capacity of a chop saw in pounds per day

ChopSawWaste.definition: Waste generated by a chop saw per day

SteelCutterCuttingCapacity.definition: Cutting capacity of a steel cutter in pounds per day

SteelCutterWaste.definition: Waste generated by a steel cutter per day

TotalCuttingRequirement.definition: Total metal cutting requirement per day in pounds

WasteLimit.definition: Maximum allowable waste per day in units

objective.description: Minimize the total number of metal-working machines (chop saws and steel cutters) needed while meeting the cutting and waste constraints.

constraints.description: 25 * (number of chop saws) + 5 * (number of steel cutters) must be greater than or equal to 520
25 * (number of chop saws) + 3 * (number of steel cutters) must be less than or equal to 400
The number of chop saws and the number of steel cutters must be nonnegative integers

ChopSaws.definition: Number of chop saws purchased by the metal-working shop

SteelCutters.definition: Number of steel cutters purchased by the metal-working shop
